opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it comes down to who this technology is actually going to serve. If you look at where most of the progress in language models has happened, it's been overwhelmingly in English, plus maybe a handful of other high-resource languages. But most of the world doesn't primarily speak English. If we're serious about this being a transformative technology, something that changes how people work, learn, and access information, then building it for only a small slice of the global population leaves a huge amount of value on the table. And frankly, it just isn't fair.

Aya came out of Cohere For AI, our research lab, and it was really a community effort. We brought together a large number of researchers and native speakers from all over the world to build datasets and models covering languages that have historically been badly underserved. A big part of the problem is data. For a lot of these languages there just isn't high-quality instruction data. So it isn't something you can fix by scaling up the same recipe. You need people who speak the language, understand the culture, and can say what a good response actually looks like.

There's also a business side, which matters to us. We work with enterprises that operate globally, and they need models that work in the languages their customers and employees speak. Multilingual capability isn't a nice-to-have for them; it's a requirement. So the research we do in the open through Aya feeds directly into making our commercial models better and more useful worldwide.

Making it open source was important too. We can't solve this alone. Releasing the data and the models lets researchers everywhere, especially in regions that don't have access to massive compute, build on that work and push it further for their own languages and communities. That compounding effect is worth far more than keeping it locked up.

So for me, it checks every box. It's the right thing to do, it's scientifically interesting and hard, and it makes our products better for the customers we care about.

r001.rationale: It says Aya releases its data and models so researchers elsewhere can build on the work and advance models for their own languages.

r002.rationale: It argues that building AI for only a small slice of the global population leaves most people without its benefits.

r003.rationale: It says useful responses require people who understand the language and culture to judge what a good response looks like.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started from a pretty simple observation: the vast majority of the world doesn't speak English, and yet almost all of the frontier work in this field has been built on English data, evaluated on English benchmarks, and optimized for English users. If you believe, as I do, that this technology is going to be one of the most important things to happen to how people access knowledge and get things done, then leaving out five or six billion people is not a minor gap. It's the whole ballgame.

So there's a values piece to it, and I don't want to downplay that. But there's also a very practical reason we invest in it heavily. The bottleneck for a lot of languages isn't compute or architecture, it's data. There just wasn't high-quality instruction data in Yoruba or Bengali or Swahili sitting around to be scraped. The only way to get it was to go to the communities who actually speak those languages and work with them. That's what Aya became: thousands of contributors across more than a hundred languages, building the dataset together. We couldn't have done that in a closed way. Open source wasn't a marketing choice, it was the only mechanism that would actually work.

And then, selfishly, it makes our models better. We serve enterprises all over the world. A bank in Japan or a government in the Middle East doesn't want a model that's fluent in English and mediocre in their language. Multilingual capability turns out to be hard to bolt on at the end. You have to care about it from the start, and the research coming out of Aya feeds directly into what we ship commercially.

The last thing I'd say is that it's good for the research community. When one or two languages dominate everything, you get a very narrow picture of what these models can and can't do. Expanding that frontier teaches us things about generalization and transfer that we wouldn't have learned otherwise. So it's one of those rare cases where the right thing to do, the commercially smart thing to do, and the scientifically interesting thing to do all line up.

r001.rationale: The response says open source enabled community-built multilingual data, but does not state that models beyond Cohere’s can use it to improve.

r002.rationale: It says that leaving out five or six billion people from this technology is “the whole ballgame,” clearly identifying the risk of excluding a large share of the global population.

r003.rationale: The response discusses languages and working with their speakers, but does not say that understanding users’ cultures is necessary for useful AI.

astra-6.text:
Because language determines who gets to use this technology. If we build models that work beautifully in English but poorly in the language you speak every day, then a huge number of people are effectively excluded from the benefits. And I don’t think translating everything into English is an adequate solution. Language carries culture and context, and you want a model that can engage with those directly.

With Aya, the investment is about expanding who these models serve and who gets to contribute to building them. That’s why the open aspect matters: people can evaluate the model in their own language, identify where it falls short, and build on it. We can’t do that well just by sitting in one lab and making assumptions about what everyone else needs.

So I see multilingual work as fundamental to making this technology useful. English performance alone is a very narrow measure of success.

r001.rationale: The response says people can evaluate and build on Aya in their own languages, but does not explain that open-sourcing its multilingual data helps models beyond Cohere’s improve.

r002.rationale: It says people are effectively excluded from AI’s benefits when models work poorly in the languages they use every day.

r003.rationale: It says language carries culture and context and that models should engage with those directly, linking that to making the technology useful.

sol-6.1.text:
Because language is how people access this technology, and if it only works well in English, you’re excluding a huge portion of the world. You’re also asking people to operate outside their own culture and context just to get the best out of a model. I don’t think that’s an acceptable outcome.

The challenge is that the data and the research effort are distributed really unevenly across languages. So you have to make a deliberate investment; you can’t just assume that progress in English will automatically carry over to everyone else. With Aya, the idea is to bring together people who actually speak these languages and understand their nuances, and make the results openly available so others can build on them.

That’s worth investing in because it expands who can participate, who can build useful applications, and whose needs shape the technology. We want this to be useful globally, and multilingual capability is fundamental to that.

r001.rationale: The response says Aya’s results are openly available so others can build on them, but does not specify that multilingual data is being open-sourced or that other language models can improve in those languages.

r002.rationale: It says that if AI works well only in English, it excludes a huge portion of the world.

r003.rationale: It says users may have to operate outside their own culture and context, and that language speakers understand nuances, but does not clearly state that AI must understand users’ cultures to be useful to them.
